title: First version of this treatise burned in the Temple of Peace fire
summary: Galen says his earlier version of the work, two books already published, was stored in a warehouse on the Sacred Way and destroyed when the precinct of Peace and the great Palatine libraries burned.
quote: left behind in the storehouse on the Sacred Way together with the others, when the whole precinct of Peace was burned, and the great libraries on the Palatine as well.
note: Outside knowledge: this is the fire of AD 192, also described in Galen's De indolentia. 'Storehouse' renders ἀποθήκῃ.

title: Lost first edition: no friend in Rome had copies
summary: All of Galen's books in that storehouse perished, and none of his friends in Rome admitted to having copies of the first two books, so companions pressed him to write the treatise again.
quote: none of my friends in [363] Rome acknowledged having copies of the first two. Since, then, my companions pressed me to write the same treatise again
note: Explains why the extant De compositione medicamentorum per genera is a second redaction.

title: On the Power of Simple Drugs cited as eleven books
summary: Galen refers readers to his commentaries On the Power of Simple Drugs and gives their number as eleven.
quote: all such matters have been defined by us in the commentaries On the Power of Simple Drugs, which are eleven in number
note: The extant De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis ac facultatibus has eleven books, which fits.

title: Reading list of Galen's pathological and therapeutic works
summary: Galen lists works his companions already have: on the differences of diseases, of symptoms, on causes of diseases, three on causes of symptoms, On Plethora, On the Differences of Fevers and the Therapeutic Method.
quote: You also have my writing On Plethora and that On the Differences of Fevers; and after these, the books of the Therapeutic Method
note: A useful internal cross-reference list for dating; all these works are extant.

title: Lost work defending solecisms against Atticist critics
summary: Galen says he showed, in writings against people who censure those who commit solecisms, that the Attic writers themselves followed prevailing usage.
quote: it has been shown [408] by me, in my writings against those who censure people who commit solecisms, that the Attic men themselves too followed the prevailing usage.
note: Outside knowledge: this polemic against hyper-Atticists does not survive; it appears in Galen's own lists of his writings.

title: Returned from Alexandria to Pergamum at age 28
summary: Galen says he devised his treatment of nerve (tendon) wounds while still young, when he first came back from Alexandria to his native city in his twenty-eighth year.
quote: I devised the regimen of treatment for those wounded in the nerves while still young, when I first returned from Alexandria to my native city, being in my twenty-eighth year.
note: Key autobiographical datum (c. AD 157). Greek γεγονὼς ἔτος ὄγδοον ἐπὶ τοῖς εἴκοσι. The automatic check failed on term recall, but the draft matches the Greek here.

title: High priest of Pergamum entrusts the gladiators to the young Galen
summary: Because of his drugs, the high priest of his city entrusted the treatment of the gladiators to Galen alone, although he was only beginning his twenty-ninth year.
quote: it seemed good, I know not how, to the high priest in our city to entrust the treatment of the gladiators to me alone, although I was young in age
note: Draft 'myself cutting through the remainder of the tendon' renders ἐντέμνων, literally 'cutting into'; the sense of the surgical step is slightly uncertain.

title: Five successive high priests renewed Galen's gladiator post
summary: No gladiator died under Galen, whereas many had died in earlier years; the next high priest reappointed him after seven months (one took office at the autumn equinox, the next in high spring), and so did the third, fourth and fifth.
quote: the second high priest after the one who had then entrusted the treatment to me likewise himself entrusted to me the care of the gladiators, after an interval of seven months.
note: The seasons give the timing of the priestly terms. Outside knowledge: this is a main source for Galen's Pergamene gladiator years.

title: Physicians in the German war dissected barbarian corpses to no purpose
summary: Galen says the physicians in the German war, though allowed to dissect barbarians' bodies, learned no more than cooks know, because they lacked practice on apes.
quote: just as the physicians in the German war, although they had license to dissect the bodies of barbarians, did not learn anything more than what cooks know.
note: Outside knowledge: the Marcomannic wars of Marcus Aurelius. A rare report of dissection of human enemy corpses.

title: 'Sacred' plasters said to come from Egyptian temples
summary: The most famous tawny plaster, 'through dittany', is classed with the 'sacred' plasters like the Isis, because they are said to have been brought from the temples in Egypt.
quote: it too being one of those named 'sacred', like the Isis, since they say that they were brought from the temples in Egypt.

title: Alexandria and Egypt: castor, radish and mustard oils abundant
summary: If you are in Alexandria, melt the drug with castor oil and radish oil, which are most plentiful there and in all Egypt; mustard oil is also easily had there.
quote: if you happen to be in Alexandria, with castor oil and radish oil, for these are most abundant in that city, as indeed throughout the whole of Egypt.

title: Attalus, king of the Pergamenes, devoted to drugs
summary: Galen says the white plaster with pepper was composed many years ago by Attalus, 'king of us Pergamenes', a man devoted to drugs of every kind; Galen doubts a better one of its kind exists.
quote: already many years ago by Attalus, who was king of us Pergamenes, a man who devoted himself to drugs of every kind
note: Outside knowledge: Attalus III Philometor (d. 133 BC), known for his work on poisons and drugs. Note Galen's 'us Pergamenes'.

title: Heras's drug book titled Narthex or Tonos of Remedies
summary: Heras recorded the Attalic plaster in his book of drugs, which some entitle Narthex and others 'Tonos of remedies'; he wanted old oil and an equal or half amount of water.
quote: Heras too mentions it in his book of drugs, which some entitle Narthex, others Tonos of Remedies
note: Heras of Cappadocia's work is lost and known mostly from Galen's quotations.

title: Mnasaeus's plaster: oil, litharge and fat in equal parts
summary: The drug compounded by Mnasaeus has oil, litharge and fat in equal amounts and is very well suited to beginning and increasing inflammations; Galen's phoinikine adds astringents to it.
quote: At any rate the drug which Mnaseas compounded has the oil, the litharge and the fat in equal amounts to one another
note: The Greek spells the name Μνασαῖος (Mnasaeus); the draft writes 'Mnaseas' here and 'Mnasaeus' elsewhere.

title: Xenocrates used the Ariobarzanian white plaster on a tarsus abscess
summary: Heras records 'the white Ariobarzanian, with which Xenocrates dispersed the abscess around the tarsus when it had already undergone change.'
quote: The white Ariobarzanian, with which Xenocrates dispersed the abscess around the tarsus when it had already undergone change.
note: Name of the plaster probably honours a king Ariobarzanes (Cappadocia); Xenocrates possibly Xenocrates of Aphrodisias. Both identifications are outside knowledge.

title: Asclepiades Pharmakion: ten books of remedies plus theriacs and women's
summary: Heras wrote one book of remedies; Asclepiades surnamed Pharmakion wrote ten, besides those on theriacs and women's remedies; Andromachus gathered nearly as many in three books: external, internal and eye remedies.
quote: Asclepiades, surnamed Pharmakion, wrote ten, apart from those on the theriacs and on women's remedies
note: Asclepiades Pharmakion (1st c. AD) is lost except through Galen.

title: Asclepiades's book titles: Marcella (external) and Mason (internal)
summary: Asclepiades entitled his five books of external remedies Marcella I to V and his five books of internal remedies Mason I to V.
quote: He himself entitles these books the first Marcella, and the second, third, fourth and fifth, just as he entitles the other five, those of the internal remedies, the first Mason
note: Compare K13.642-643, where the Greek assigns 'Marcellas' to the internal remedies (see doubt item).

title: Pamphileion: Asclepiades renamed the Attalic plaster after its user
summary: Asclepiades calls the white pepper plaster not Attalic but Pamphileion; Galen thinks he did not know its inventor and named it after the man who used it and gave it to him.
quote: does not call it Attalic but Pamphileion, being ignorant, as [447] I think, of the one who first discovered it, and having added instead the name of the man who used it and gave it to him.
note: Shows how recipe names drift between collections.

title: Mantias the Herophilean, first compiler of drug recipes
summary: The first author Galen knows who wrote up many praiseworthy compound drugs was Mantias the Herophilean; his pupil Heraclides of Tarentum imitated him in drugs and in dietetics.
quote: first of those I know, by Mantias the Herophilean, whose pupil Heraclides of Tarentum appears to imitate him not only in the use of drugs but also in the dietetic part of the art.
note: Both works are lost; this is a key statement on the origins of Greek recipe collections.

title: Canon of pharmacologists: Musa, Heras, Andromachus, Asclepiades, Criton, Archigenes
summary: Mantias and Heraclides wrote first; recipes were sifted by experience; most successful afterwards were Petronius Musa, Heras, Andromachus, Asclepiades and Criton, and Archigenes and Philippus also wrote many.
quote: Among these, those who seem most to have achieved success in the experience of drugs are Petronius Musa and Heras and Andromachus, and Asclepiades and Criton.
note: Note the name form 'Petronius Musa'; compare 'Petronas' in K13.641-642.

title: Menecrates's book 'Autokrator hologrammatos' of noteworthy drugs
summary: Galen cites one book by Menecrates titled 'Autokrator hologrammatos of noteworthy drugs' and says he will also include drugs used by his own teachers.
quote: And there is also one book of Menecrates entitled [503] 'Autokrator hologrammatos (The Emperor, written out in full letters) of noteworthy drugs'.
note: Outside knowledge: Menecrates (Ti. Claudius Menecrates) wrote quantities in full words to prevent copying errors; the work is lost.

title: Damocrates's recipes in iambic trimeter preserve proportions
summary: Galen quotes Damocrates's white plaster in his own verses because recipes written in metre are easy to remember and keep their proportions exact.
quote: Since the compositions of drugs written down in metre are easy to remember and preserve their proportions exactly, it seemed to me better to make mention of these too.
note: Damocrates (Servilius Damocrates, 1st c. AD) verse recipes survive largely through Galen.

title: Criton's fourth book of Drugs: 'boxwood-coloured' plasters
summary: Criton calls quince-yellow plasters 'boxwood-coloured' (pyxinai) and wrote others in the fourth book of his Drugs.
quote: Criton has also written certain other plasters in the fourth book of his Drugs, 'boxwood-coloured' as he himself names them, but 'quince-yellow' according to the [517] others

title: Galen searched all drug writers for a contemporary's recipe
summary: Galen could not find a contemporary physician's metallic nerve drug in Asclepiades Pharmakion, Petronas, Andromachus, Heras, Mantias, Heraclides, Archigenes, Philippus, Soranus, Menecrates, Crito or Damocrates.
quote: having read everything written on drugs by Soranus and Menecrates and Crito and Damocrates and the others who hold a reputation for knowledge of drugs, in none of them did I find this drug
note: Shows what pharmacological library Galen had; Soranus's drug writings are otherwise lost.

title: Dioscorides of Anazarbus quoted on ranking resins
summary: Galen quotes Dioscorides, On Materials book 1, ranking terebinth first among resins, then mastic, pine, fir, peuke and strobilos, and reconciles it with his own ranking by heat.
quote: Of all the resins the terebinth takes first place, and after it the mastic (schinine), then the pine (pityine) and the fir (elatine), after which are counted the peuke-pine (peukine) and the strobilos (pine-cone) resin.
note: Dioscorides is extant (De materia medica 1.71); a check on Galen's quotation practice.

title: Andromachus's white plaster quoted from 'Remedies for External Conditions'
summary: Galen quotes Andromachus's own white plaster: litharge and white lead one mina each, wax and resin a quarter, oil three kotylai, water two kotylai, with no uses or boiling given.
quote: The white plaster which I use: litharge, one mina; white lead, one mina; wax, a quarter; resin, a quarter; oil, three kotylai; water, two kotylai.
note: Andromachus the Younger's work survives only in Galen's quotations.

title: Lucius 'the Teacher' used Asclepiades's cadmia plaster
summary: In Asclepiades's list of cicatrizing plasters the cadmia plaster is noted as used by 'Lucius the Teacher', who elsewhere is called 'our teacher Lucius'.
quote: The cicatrizing plaster through cadmia. Lucius the Teacher used this.
note: The words are Asclepiades's, so Lucius was Asclepiades's teacher, not Galen's (compare K13.538-539).

title: Rusticus, pupil of Isidorus, variant of Heraclides's plaster
summary: For Heraclides's quince-yellow plaster dispersing internal abscesses, Galen gives a variant 'according to Rusticus, the pupil of Isidorus'.
quote: But according to Rusticus, the pupil of Isidorus
note: These two physicians are otherwise obscure.

title: Pythion's fracture plaster used by Helenus; bathe with it on
summary: Asclepiades records the fracture plaster of Pythion, used by Helenus, so adhesive that it must be loosened with a hot wet sponge; the patient should bathe with the drug on.
quote: Another, the fracture-plaster of Pythion. Helenus used this.
note: Contains Judaean asphalt and Bruttian pitch.

title: Claudius Philoxenus the surgeon: 'Egyptian' plaster
summary: Asclepiades gives the Egyptian plaster of Claudius Philoxenus the surgeon, with litharge, wax, ammoniac, propolis, copper and steel flake, burnt greasy wool and castor oil.
quote: The Egyptian of Claudius Philoxenus the surgeon, for the aforementioned conditions.
note: Outside knowledge: Claudius Philoxenus was an Alexandrian surgeon also cited by Celsus. Another plaster of his is at K13.538-539.

title: Unnamed rich man worth 500 myriads demands costly drugs
summary: Galen tells of an unnamed rich man, worth no more than five hundred myriads, a lover of drugs and of medicine, who scorned cheap remedies. He is the same man Galen mentions without a name in book 1 of On Prognosis from the Pulse.
quote: where a man possessing not more than five hundred myriads, a lover of drugs and a lover of medicine, did not think fit to use any of the cheap ones
note: 500 myriads, probably of sesterces or drachmas, is a large fortune; the unit is not stated.

title: Two physicians ruined by losing their recipe books
summary: Galen knew two physicians who lost their written recipes: one wasted away from grief and died, the other gave up medical practice.
quote: for the one, wasted away by grief at the loss of such writings, died, while the other withdrew from medical practice.
note: Galen's stated reason for teaching a method of compounding rather than a list. Compare his De indolentia on losses in the fire.

title: Galen's phoinikine (date-palm) plaster: exact quantities
summary: Galen's own chalcitis plaster: old unsalted fat (sellers call it axoungion) 2 litrai, old oil 3 litrai, litharge 3 litrai, chalcitis 4 ounces, stirred with a fresh palm-wood stick.
quote: Of the old fat, which those who sell it call axoungion, let there be 2 litrai; of the old oil, 3 litrai; and of litharge, 3 litrai; and of chalcitis, 4 ounces.
note: Outside knowledge: the 'diachalciteos' plaster became the medieval diapalma. 'Axoungion' is Latin axungia, a trade term.

title: Attalic white plaster with white pepper: full composition
summary: Litharge and white lead one litra each, oil two litrai by measure, wax half a litra, terebinth 3 ounces, frankincense half or equal to that, split alum 6 drachms, white pepper 3; the metals are boiled in the sun first.
quote: In addition to these, half a litra of wax by weight, three ounces of terebinth resin, of frankincense either half of this or an amount equal to it, and six drachmas of alum and three of pepper.

title: Heras's white plaster for rabid-dog bites, also as pills
summary: Heras's white plaster for hydrophobes: white Pontic wax 2 lb, chrysitis litharge 1 lb, white lead 1 lb, myrrh and deer marrow 2 oz each, frankincense 1 oz, old oil 1 xestes. For severe cases a pill the size of a Pontic nut is given for forty days.
quote: one should also make from it a pill the size of a Pontic nut and give it, and [432] do this for forty days.
note: Galen will not test it on rabies (K13.435-436).

title: Asclepiades's 'Rhodian' plaster for hard breasts, with egg yolks
summary: Asclepiades's Rhodian plaster, discutient for hardnesses of the breasts: litharge and Pontic wax one litra each, white lead and pig's fat half a litra each, myrrh 4 ounces, two roasted egg yolks, 1.5 kotylai oil.
quote: of myrrh four ounces, of roasted eggs two yolks, and one and a half kotylai of oil.

title: Green plaster of Gallus, first of Andromachus's green series
summary: Andromachus's first green plaster, of Gallus: pine-cone resin 300 dr, wax 100 dr, scraped verdigris 50 dr, frankincense 25 dr, vinegar as needed. Galen judges it drying, for large wounds and hard ulcers.
quote: Green plaster of Gallus. Rx: pine-cone resin, 300 drachmas; wax, 100 drachmas; scraped verdigris, 50 drachmas.

title: Isis green plaster as recorded by Epigonus, with dracontium
summary: The plaster others call Isis, written by Andromachus as Epigonus's green plaster: equal parts burnt copper, ammoniac salt, copper scale, verdigris, ammoniac, aristolochia, frankincense, with aloe, myrrh, galbanum, round alum, Colophonian resin and wax. Epigonus added dracontium root.
quote: He added this at the end, since it is not carried in the recipe of the Isis; for Epigonus added it, and in this respect the Isis of Epigonus differed.
note: The Isis is one of the 'Egyptian' sacred plasters (K13.517-518).

title: Galen's tawny plaster of metals only, with old Sabine oil
summary: Galen's own tawny plaster without resin or wax: 4 litrai of oil (the older the better, especially Sabine), 3 litrai litharge, 2 of sharpest vinegar, and 2 ounces each of black copper scale, verdigris and chalcitis.
quote: I put in four litrai of oil—and the older it is, the better it will be, and all the more if it is Sabine—and three litrai of litharge.
note: Continues in K13.519-520 with uses: glues bleeding wounds, closes fistulas.

title: Heras's three-ingredient cephalic troche ground in the dog-days
summary: Heras's 'trimigma' troche for skull fractures: erythrias earth, red copper scale and Pontic fish-glue, ground with sharp vinegar for 20 days in the dog-day heat, then sunned 8 days in a red-copper vessel.
quote: Do this in the heats of the dog-days for 20 days. Then take the fish-glue, crush it, pour on 1 kotyle of vinegar and melt it over a gentle fire

title: Caunian white plaster with hyena fat and deer rennet
summary: A white plaster called Caunian: white wax, myrrh, frankincense, deer marrow, hyena fat, deer (or kid) rennet, nitre, galbanum, ammoniac, litharge, white lead, old oil and sea-water.
quote: of hyena's fat, 2 ounces; of deer's rennet, 2 ounces, or of kid's

title: Halieus's tawny plaster against stingray and weever wounds
summary: Asclepiades's tawny plaster of Halieus is for bleeding wounds, cut nerves, breast indurations, dog and human bites, and wounds from sea stingrays, weevers and other dangerous fish.
quote: It works excellently also for the strikes of sea stingrays and weevers and the other dangerous fishes.
note: 'Weevers' renders δρακόντων (sea-dragons, i.e. weever fish).

title: Moschion's fracture plaster: dropsy, bronchocele, corns
summary: Moschion's fracture plaster claims to form callus on bones, help incipient dropsy and testicle contusions, shrink piles, dissolve bronchoceles and remove 'nails' (corns) without ulceration; the mina is set at 160 drachms.
quote: It is effective also against the callus-like outgrowths on the feet and hands, which we call "nails" (hēloi), so as to remove them without ulceration

title: Heras's black barbaros spread on two leathers for blood-spitting
summary: Heras's black plaster for bleeding wounds also stanches blood in those who bring up blood: spread on two pieces of leather, one on chest and sides, one on the back. Change it every 7 days in winter, 5 in summer.
quote: Having spread it onto two pieces of leather, apply one [558] to the chest and the sides, and the other to the back; it checks the blood remarkably.

title: Galen's barbaros plaster for the greatest wounds
summary: Galen gives his own barbaros: pitch 8 litrai, wax 6 litrai 8 oz, pine resin 5 litrai 4 oz, asphalt 4 litrai, oil, plus litharge, white lead, verdigris, frankincense, alums, opopanax, aloe, opium, myrrh, terebinth, mandrake juice and 6 cotylae vinegar.
quote: They are two: one for the greatest wounds, another for the smaller ones.
note: For the oil quantity see the doubt item on σι΄.

title: Costly fragrant nerve-wound drug made for a rich patron
summary: For the rich man Galen made a nerve drug of cinnamon, dittany and maron (40 dr each), with a little amaracus because it was hard to get in Rome, in a cerate of the best opobalsam and Tyrrhenian wax.
quote: Take of cinnamon, dittany and maron, forty drachms of each; for these are fragrant and fine-particled.
note: Shows luxury pharmacy for elite clients; compare the cheap rustic remedies in K13.582-584.

title: Strongest and weakest metallic drugs for nerve punctures
summary: Strongest: raw chalcitis 1, raw misy 2, copper scale 3 parts. Weakest: burnt misy and chalcitis 1 each, scale 4. Middle: burnt misy, chalcitis and verdigris 1 each, scale 3. Wax is added at 2 to 2.5 times the metals.
quote: let it have one part of raw chalcitis, two of misy, likewise raw, and three of scale of copper; and the weakest, likewise one of misy and of chalcitis, but both burnt, and four of the scale.
note: The worked example gives 12 parts of wax for both the strongest and the weakest, though the rule (double vs two and a half) needs 15 for the weakest; the Greek has the same ιβ΄, so the numeral is corrupt in the text, and the following 'between eighteen and twelve' is also confused.

title: Oily pitch in vinegar keeps rabid-bite wounds open
summary: Galen's drug for rabid dog bites is oily pitch boiled in sharp vinegar (one Roman sextarius vinegar, one litra pitch, three ounces opopanax); it stops the wound closing and suits hard bodies such as diggers and reapers.
quote: This drug does not allow the wound of those bitten by rabid dogs to cicatrize.

title: Fistulous thigh healed overnight under the phoinikine
summary: A youth's thigh suppurated near the groin and became fistulous under the skin. Galen planned to cut it near the kneecap, but on the day of the operation it was found dry and closed, so he kept using the drug.
quote: But when the thigh was unbound on the following day, on which I had resolved to cut it, everything was found to have fallen together, dry and without moisture.

title: Farmer's boy with a parotid fistula cured by litharge plaster
summary: In the country Galen gave a 15-year-old farmer's son a litharge-vinegar-oil plaster for a six-month fistula left after a parotid swelling; he forgot the case, and two months later the boy came back healed.
quote: For the boy was a farmer's son, about fifteen years of age
note: A pig's bristle was used as a probe; a second similar boy was then cured.

title: Pankratiast bitten on the index finger nearly lost it
summary: Someone persuaded a physician to apply the Attalic white plaster to a young man bitten on the index finger in the pankration; putrefaction set in and the finger was agglutinated only with difficulty.
quote: a young man who had been bitten on the index finger in the pankration, who was in such a bad state that the whole bitten part was in danger of rotting away
note: Biting was forbidden in the pankration, so this detail is notable (outside knowledge).

title: Improvised verdigris cerate in a village without drugs
summary: In a village with no drugs Galen found only verdigris and wax; he melted the wax with rose oil and added verdigris at one twelfth, and both 1/10 and 1/12 proved right for different bodies.
quote: I myself once did in a certain village, in which I neither had any drug with me myself, nor was anyone else among the people there well supplied

title: Asclepiades: 'the Best' plaster held loose bone fragments
summary: Asclepiades reports using his black fracture plaster 'the Best' on fractures with many floating bone fragments; when everyone advised removing them, the plaster made them form callus with the rest.
quote: I used this drug in the case of fractures in which many bones were floating loose, and when all were advising me to lift out the floating ones, 'the Best' accomplished something resembling a marvel.
note: The first person is Asclepiades, quoted verbatim by Galen.

title: Contused middle finger: tendon thought rotten was preserved
summary: A young man's contused middle finger was putrefying; Galen used lye with raw barley meal, then bitter-vetch. A half-rotten sinewy membrane came away, which onlookers took for the whole nerve, but the tendon was intact.
quote: It seemed, then, to all those who saw it that this body was the whole nerve, rotted through, since they did not know how these tendons, clothed in sinewy membranes, both pass forward through the wrist
note: The troche of Polyeides dissolved in hepsema was used next.

title: Euphorbium cerate invented for a chilled knee, sent to the bath
summary: In a hard winter a man with a knee that hurt when chilled asked for a heating drug and said he would send for it from the bath. Galen improvised euphorbium ground in oil with melted wax, and the man was soon free of pain.
quote: "Now then," he said, "I am going off to bathe, and I shall send for the drug from the bath."
note: Origin story of Galen's euphorbium cerate.

title: Nerve-wounded man relapsed after going out in the cold
summary: On day four, pain-free, a nerve-wounded patient went out in great cold on business and came home with the limb tense up to the neck. Galen bathed it in hot oil and applied liquid euphorbium with castoreum, and by evening the symptoms had stopped.
quote: went out of the house in great cold for some necessary business, and having spent a longer time at it, came home with the whole limb strained with tension as far as the neck and feeling great pain.

title: Old euphorbium worked; an imitator's fresh euphorbium burned
summary: Galen had a servant apply 5–6-year-old euphorbium in old oil to a tendon puncture, and it healed. An onlooker used fresh euphorbium the same way on another man, causing heat, biting and pain; Galen switched to the vinegar drug.
quote: I gave one of my people old euphorbium and ordered him to triturate it with old oil to the thickness of a liquid cerate and to apply it to the puncture of the tendon in the hand.

title: Country improvisations for nerve wounds: propolis, leaven, spurge
summary: On journeys and in the country Galen treated nerve wounds with what was at hand: a farmer's fresh propolis, old leaven, both mixed, or leaven with juice of spurge growing near the farmyard.
quote: In the case of another countryman I mixed the juice of spurge with the leaven and applied it, having seen it growing near his farmyard; for I had judged the leaven deficient as being fresh.

title: Farmer copied Galen's pigeon-dung remedy for nerve wounds
summary: Galen once used acrid dung of pigeons from country towers on a nerve-wounded young man; the farmer managing the estate, 'not unintelligent', copied it and has used it on nerve wounds ever since.
quote: And the farmer who had charge of this estate, having observed this — for he was not unintelligent — imitated it and always uses it and treats those who have been wounded in the nerves.

title: Schoolboy stabbed with a stylus died of spasm on day seven
summary: The best Empiricist of Galen's day, who had read all the anatomists, treated a schoolchild stabbed in the inner upper arm with a stylus; the child seemed well but died in convulsions on the seventh day.
quote: when a child at school had once made a stab with a stylus into the inner region of the upper arm, above its middle parts, applied one of the plaster drugs
note: Galen then explained the error (K13.605-606): a narrow puncture over a nerve needs a fine, heating drug and an open mouth.

title: Rich man's slave cured cheaply: 'keep this for beggars'
summary: The rich man failed to treat his slave's malignant ulcer, sent him to Galen, then asked for the recipe; hearing all the ingredients were cheap, he said to keep it for beggars and teach him a costly one.
quote: 'this,' he said, 'keep for beggars; but teach me one of the more costly ones.'
note: The draft has a garbled phrase ('not even (μὴ γοῦν μήτε) when the one who applied it...') just before; the Greek may be corrupt there.

title: Rich patron had free men and slaves find nerve-wounded test patients
summary: After getting Galen's costly recipes, the rich man ordered his free men and slaves to find people with nerve wounds to try them; the drugs worked and he honoured Galen with gifts.
quote: ordered both his freemen and his slaves to seek out for him persons with wounded nerves.
note: Greek ἐλευθέροις means free men (the draft's 'freemen'), not freedmen. Testing on recruited patients is a striking social detail.

title: Teachers' wet treatment of gladiators' knee tendons killed most
summary: Galen saw his teachers treat gladiators wounded at the kneecap tendon with hot water and wheat-flour poultices in water-and-oil; very few survived, and those were lamed.
quote: But perhaps it would be better to say not being treated, but perishing; for very few of them survived, and these became lame.
note: Unit failed the automatic check; the sense is clear in the Greek.

title: Stirring the plaster with a fresh palm branch
summary: The phoinikine is stirred with the thick end of a fresh palm branch, and thin peeled pieces are thrown in at the cerate stage to add their juice; the branch is cut the day before in winter, the same day in summer.
quote: So, if it is winter, let it be removed on the previous day; but in summer the branch must be removed from the tree on that very day on which you boil the drug.
note: The palm juice is the 'date' (φοῖνιξ) element of the plaster's name.

title: Hernia surgeons apply the plaster right after operating
summary: Many who operate on hernias apply the phoinikine immediately after surgery, without even moistening the wound first, to prevent inflammation.
quote: many of those who operate on hernias also apply it immediately after the surgery, carrying through the treatment with it together with the affusions and the poultices.

title: Rectal injection by horn tube fitted with a pig's bladder
summary: For inflamed swellings of the seat and rectum, the plaster is melted with more oil, in a water bath over smokeless coals, and injected through a straight-bored horn with a pig's bladder tied on.
quote: so that it can be injected through a straight-bored horn having a pig's bladder fastened to it, as we are accustomed to use in such cases.
note: A simple clyster device; also used for sinuses (K13.499-500).

title: Teacher smeared wild pigeon blood on wounds before plastering
summary: One of Galen's teachers smeared sinuses and large fresh wounds with the blood of 'grazing' pigeons living in field towers, not domestic ones, before applying the wine plaster.
quote: smearing beforehand with the blood of a pigeon, not of the domestic ones, [515] but of those called by some boskades (the 'grazing' ones), which go into the towers that people in our country construct in the fields.
note: 'In our country' means Galen's Asia Minor.

title: Storing gathered herbs: dry rooms with south-facing windows
summary: Herbs should be watched through their fruiting stages to learn when to gather them, and stored in dry rooms, not underground, not under tiles, with windows facing south, away from sun-baking and damp.
quote: This would come about if the rooms are neither underground nor προσχόρων (adjoining the ground?), nor under tiles, having, however, their windows turned toward the south.
note: The draft leaves προσχόρων untranslated with a guess; the word is rare and uncertain.

title: Test a new euphorbium plaster on your own shin or forearm
summary: If unsure of the euphorbium's strength, spread a little of the plaster on linen and apply it to your own shin or forearm for some hours, then weaken it with cerate or strengthen it with euphorbium.
quote: spread a little of what has been prepared on a linen cloth and apply it to your own shin or forearm for some hours
note: A rare explicit self-test of drug strength.

title: Nerve-wound regimen: warm oil, never water, dressing changed twice daily
summary: Galen keeps water away from nerve wounds altogether, washing off blood with oil; he unbinds and foments with sufficiently warm oil two or three times a day, at dawn and evening, and at night when nights are long.
quote: I guard against the use of water throughout the whole treatment, to the point that it does not even touch the wound

title: Letting the nerve-wounded bathe: oiled linen over the plaster
summary: Since patients insist on bathing, Galen puts a plaster on the wound, several oil-soaked folded linens and a linen bandage over it, and pours oil on the bandage just before the patient steps into the tub.
quote: I first pour the oil over the bandage, when the person wounded in the nerves is about to step into the tub
note: The Greek reads εἰς τὴν πτύελον (spittle), surely a corruption of πύελον (tub); the draft silently translates 'tub', correctly.

title: Deep sutures for a transverse thigh wound in a gladiator 'horseman'
summary: For a gladiator of the 'horsemen' class with a deep transverse wound above the kneecap, Galen dropped the usual treatment and sutured the muscles deep, after freeing the tendons; his teachers sewed only skin or the muscle surface.
quote: I ventured, departing from the treatment named 'according to breadth' (kata platos), to bring together with sutures the separated parts of the muscles toward one another.
note: Hippeis (mounted gladiators) is a known gladiator class.

title: Cross-incision to keep a narrow nerve puncture open
summary: For narrow punctures over a nerve, keep the opening open so the hot drug can draw out the moisture; if needed enlarge it with two skin incisions crossing at right angles.
quote: with two incisions through the skin cutting one another at right angles.

title: Making hepsema/siraion: last-run must from sweetest grapes
summary: Siraion (boiled must) for dissolving troches should be made from the sweetest grapes and the last-flowing must, boiled to half; must of another kind is boiled down to a third.
quote: And it becomes such when the must is neither from austere grapes, [613] but from grapes as sweet as possible, nor from what flows first, but from what flows last.

title: Bath test of euphorbium unguent strength
summary: Galen's test unguent is euphorbium 1, wax 3, oil 12. Rubbed on the body it shows the drug's strength, especially in the bath, where fresh strong euphorbium makes the skin sting in the air and even more in the water.
quote: And it becomes most evident in the bath; for people are stung strongly, by the air indeed, but still more by the water, when the euphorbium is hot and new and strong.

title: Cretan henbane and mandrake juice shipped to Rome yearly
summary: Henbane juice put up in summer is brought to Rome from Crete every year, and the finest mandrake juice also comes from Crete in earthenware cups.
quote: Know that this too is brought from Crete, of the finest quality, in earthenware cups.
note: Galen elsewhere describes the Cretan herb trade for the imperial court (outside knowledge).

title: Fine wines for drugs: Ariousian, Lesbian, Tmolite, Falernian
summary: Substitutes for Falernian: the Ariousian of Chios, the fragrant Lesbian (little at Mitylene, more and better at Eresos and Methymna), and the Tmolite, which resembles Falernian; a second Tmolite is dry and astringent.
quote: the very fragrant Lesbian, which is produced in small quantity at Mitylene, but at Eresos and Methymna is at once both more abundant and better, and the Tmolite, which resembles the Falernian.

title: Ariusian wine once used for antidotes, now Falernian
summary: The finest tawny wines 'among us in Asia' are the Tmolite, the Lesbian and the Ariusian of Chios, which everyone once used for the finest drugs and antidotes, as they now use Falernian.
quote: the one most renowned among the ancients, the Ariusian, which is produced in Chios, which everyone used to use for the finest of the drugs and especially [514] for the antidotes, just as now they use the Falernian.

title: 'Pontic' wax as a trade name for any white wax
summary: Naturally white wax is called Pontic even when it comes from elsewhere, because Pontus produces the most; Tyrrhenian wax is not naturally white.
quote: Naturally white is the so-called Pontic wax—for it is now customarily so named even if it comes from some other region, because white wax is produced in the greatest quantity in Pontus

title: Rhodian white lead imitated by makers at Puteoli
summary: For a very white plaster use Rhodian white lead; some white-lead makers at Puteoli, formerly Dicaearchia, make theirs white in the same way.
quote: in the city formerly named Dicaearchia and now Puteoli, some of those who prepare white lead are accustomed to make it white in the same way as the Rhodian.
note: Evidence for white-lead (cerussa) manufacture at Puteoli.

title: Roman litra: same name for weight and for horn liquid measure
summary: At Rome the litra of weight for solids has the same name as the litra measure for liquids, a very common horn vessel found throughout the whole city.
quote: For among the Romans the litra weight of solid bodies is called by the same name as the litra measure of liquids, which is very common throughout the whole city, being made of horn material.

title: Oil measured by a horn litra marked in twelve ounces
summary: Romans measure oil with a horn vessel incised with lines into twelve parts; the whole is a litra and each part an ounce, distinct from the weight ounce used on the balance for metals and wax.
quote: There is among them a measure, with which they measure oil, incised with lines that divide the whole into twelve parts; and the whole measure is called by them a litra, and the twelfth part of it an ounce.

title: Roman xestes = 20 measure-ounces; horn measures with rings
summary: The xestes name spread to all Greek-speakers under Roman rule, but the measure varies; the Roman xestes holds 1 2/3 litrai, i.e. 20 ounces, measured with horns marked with circular lines. Some wrongly say 18.
quote: Among the Romans, at any rate, the xestes contains one litra and a half and a sixth, so that the ounces in all are twenty; and these they for the most part measure with the horns
note: Important metrological testimony.

title: Old recipes' kotyle equals nine Roman ounces
summary: Some say the mina has 20 ounces, others 16. From old recipes written before Roman dominance Galen infers that their kotyle equals nine ounces of the litra now used in Rome.
quote: I have conjectured that what those authors call a kotyle is equal to nine of the ounces that make up the litra now in use in Rome.
note: Compare K13.429-430 (some say 16 2/3 ounces) and K13.434-435 (Roman xestes 20).

title: Andromachus at Rome still wrote kotylai, not local litrai
summary: Galen wonders why Andromachus, living in Rome, wrote kotylai instead of the local units litra, xestes and ounce.
quote: And yet one might wonder how, while residing in Rome, he named kotylai instead of litrai; for these are the local names: that of the litra, that of the xestes, and that of the ounce.

title: Alexandrian mina of 20 ounces = 160 drachms
summary: Where Asclepiades says the mina has 160 drachms, Galen infers the Alexandrian mina of 20 ounces at 8 drachms each.
quote: It is quite evident, then, that he means the Alexandrian mina, which has 20 ounces, so that each of the ounces has 8 drachmas

title: Colophonian frankincense-scented resin: scarce and costly
summary: The frankincense-like Colophonian resin, which some call the only true Colophonian, smells pleasant and heats moderately; it is produced in very small quantity and is therefore expensive.
quote: It is produced in very small quantity, and for this reason it is costly.

title: Hard bodies of farmers, sailors and hunters need stronger drugs
summary: Galen calls 'stronger' the drier bodies of farmers, sailors and hunters, and 'weaker' the soft bodies of women, eunuchs and children.
quote: those that are drier in their temperaments, such as are those of farmers, sailors and hunters; by weaker, those that are softer by nature or by habit, such as those of women, eunuchs and children

title: Powerful patrons order plasters by colour
summary: Because some very powerful men order a quince-yellow plaster for a given purpose, later physicians grouped plasters by colour and added their uses.
quote: some of the very powerful men sometimes order us to make for them a quince-yellow plaster that is agglutinative of wounds, or cicatrizing, or emollient of parts that are becoming hardened
note: Explains the colour-based arrangement of recipe books such as Andromachus's.

title: Menoetus's 'pugilistic' plaster used by boxers
summary: Menoetus's first quince-yellow plaster is called 'pugilistic' because boxers in particular use it.
quote: the one called the 'pugilistic' plaster, because boxers in particular use the drug
note: Confirms the label 'for boxers (πυκτική)' on Serapion's plaster in K13.509.

title: Drug adulteration by root-cutters, merchants and pedlars
summary: Galen has the finest drugs sent to him yearly from each nation because petty-ware sellers corrupt them; worse are the merchants who carry them, and worst the root-cutters bringing roots, juices, fruits and flowers down from the mountains.
quote: For you know how the finest drugs are conveyed to me from each of the nations every year, because the wretched sellers of petty wares (ῥωποπῶλαι) corrupt them in every possible way.
note: A key passage on the ancient drug supply chain.

title: Pedlars sell liquid pine resin as terebinth
summary: Dealers in sundries sell liquid pine resin in place of terebinth to buyers who cannot tell them apart; it is sharper in smell, taste and power.
quote: similar in consistency to the liquid pine resin, which the dealers in sundries sell in place of terebinth to those who do not know how to distinguish them.

title: Everyone, even country folk, now bathes daily; rich patients disobey
summary: Galen complains that endurance has perished: even country people bathe every day; the poor mostly obey orders, but the rich and powerful are hard to persuade or disobey, so it would be best not to treat them.
quote: But since in present-day life endurance has perished among all men, so that by now even those in the fields have become accustomed to bathe every day

title: Cyrenaic juice weakened since growers irrigate for yield
summary: Fresh euphorbium heats more than Cyrenaic juice, especially present-day Cyrenaic, since growers water the plants to make them grow and yield more juice.
quote: especially more than that of the present day, ever since they have been making the plants grow by watering with water and preparing them for an abundant production of juice
note: Outside knowledge: Cyrenaic juice is silphium; this is rare evidence of its cultivation in Galen's time, after Pliny reported it extinct. The draft links 'after one year' to the euphorbium, which the Greek supports.

title: Regional resin names: Laconian 'first-flowing', Cilician kapnelaion
summary: Self-flowing resins are called 'first-flowing' in Lacedaemon and elsewhere, and kapnelaion in Cilicia; unrefined pine resin is shipped in cases and jars full of wood and stones.
quote: In Lacedaemon and in certain other places they call these 'first-flowing' (πρωτόρρυτοι), while in Cilicia they name such a resin kapnelaion (smoke-oil)
note: Unit failed the automatic check. The Greek spells the word πρωτοῤῥύτους. 'Smoke-oil' is the draft's gloss.

title: Black amaracine perfume once made with Pontic pitch
summary: Oily fragrant pitch from Bruttium and from Pontus was put into the black amaracine unguent, as all of it used to be made; nowadays they make a whitish amaracine without it.
quote: that brought from the regions about Pontus, which is at once oily and fragrant, and which they put into the black amaracine unguent, such as formerly all of it used to be prepared.
note: A change in perfume manufacture within Galen's lifetime (continues in K13.630).

title: Roman perfumed oils 'spicatum' and 'foliatum' and perfumers' wax
summary: For bared nerves Galen made a cerate of perfumers' wax with the perfumes the Romans call spicatum and foliatum, adding a twelfth of washed pompholyx.
quote: I compounded the cerate from the wax called perfumers' wax and from the perfumed oils named among the Romans spicatum and foliatum.
note: Latin perfume names written in Greek.

title: Emplastron with rho; kentrion and melotris etymologies
summary: Galen notes that recent physicians write emplastron with a rho, as with kentrion (from kentein, to prick) and melotris (from mele, probe, and ous, ear), and he follows the prevailing usage.
quote: the kentrion having been named from kentein (to prick), its final syllable not having the rho, and the melotris being compounded from mele (probe) and ous (ear).

title: 'Arsenikon' vs Atticists' 'arrhenikon'
summary: Galen notes physicians say arsenikon, while those who want to Atticize everything say arrhenikon; he mixed it with the tetrapharmakon as a trial.
quote: that which is called arsenikon by physicians, but arrhenikon by those who wish to Atticize everything

title: Sea-hare harms only the lung; cantharides only the bladder
summary: Against people who mock organ-specific drugs, Galen notes that sea-hare ulcerates only the lung, cantharides only the bladder, and other drugs break kidney stones or ease expectoration.
quote: by the sea-hare the lung alone of all the parts in the body is ulcerated, and the bladder alone, in turn, by cantharides

title: Mockers of organ-specific drugs quote a tragic verse
summary: Critics mocked drugs said to act on particular organs by asking whether someone orders them about as in a tragedy: 'You, go to the streams of Inachus; and you, proceed around Cadmean Thebes.'
quote: "You, go to the streams of Inachus; and you, proceed around Cadmean Thebes"?
note: The verse comes from an unnamed tragedy (outside knowledge: a fragment, sometimes attributed to Aeschylus or Sophocles); Galen does not name the author.

title: Empiricists credit compound drugs to dreams and chance; 'cephalic' example
summary: Galen says Empiricists refer nearly all compounds to dreams, chance and accident, admitting a few found by epilogismos, such as the novel 'cephalic' drug made by mixing all flesh-producing simples.
quote: the contentiousness of the Empiricist physicians, who refer nearly all compound drugs to dreams and chance and accidental encounter
note: The draft also keeps an editorial note '(μίξωμιν, read μίξωμεν)' from the Kühn text.

title: Mixing a 5th-degree and a 3rd-degree drug gives the 4th
summary: Galen's rationale for compounding: if no simple of the needed degree is available, mixing one hotter by five degrees with one hotter by three yields the mean of four.
quote: if we have at hand two, of which the one is hotter by five degrees and the other by three, by mixing them we shall produce the mean, which exceeds the well-tempered state by four degrees.
note: Note: elsewhere Galen speaks of four orders; here he counts numerical degrees.

title: Reason finds the composition, experience judges it
summary: Galen states that reason discovers the composition of a drug while experience judges its excellence, so drugs composed by art are trusted even by non-rationalists.
quote: For reason discovers the composition, but experience judges the excellence of what has been discovered

title: Rheumatic conditions come from weakness and cold, not heat
summary: Against those who think fluxes come from much heat, Galen says weakness of parts, mostly from cold dyscrasia, causes rheumatic conditions; relaxants alone make them slack, strong astringents make them scirrhous.
quote: Rather, it is the weakness of the parts that produces the rheumatic conditions, a weakness which for the most part is brought about in accordance with a cold dyscrasia.

title: Twelve grades of drug action, against Dioscorides's 'by kind'
summary: Galen insists drugs must be known not only by kind, as Dioscorides wrote, but by order (first to fourth) and position within each order (beginning, middle, end), giving twelve grades.
quote: not simply by kind, as Dioscorides wrote in a different manner, but as we did in the books on simple drugs

title: Galen refuses to test an untried drug on rabies patients
summary: Galen never tried Heras's plaster on rabid-dog bites, because he had a reliable crab remedy; abandoning sure cures in so dangerous a disease for an experiment seemed terrible and unjust.
quote: to abandon the reliable remedies in so dangerous an affection and to betray the safety of the bitten person for the sake of an officious experiment seemed to me terrible and unjust.
note: An explicit ethical limit on human experimentation. The crab remedy is described in other Galenic works (outside knowledge).

title: Galen came to value Hippocrates's 'help, or do no harm'
summary: Galen at first thought the maxim to help or not harm unworthy of Hippocrates, but changed his mind after seeing physicians admired for a drug later laughed at when it failed on other patients.
quote: a thing which I at first disdained, so as to think it not even worthy of Hippocrates when he exhorts us to do everything in the art in such a way as to help, or not to harm.
note: Epidemics I.11; a rare personal comment on the maxim.

title: Physicians drop proven ancient drugs to look original
summary: Most physicians abandon drugs proven since antiquity so as to seem to have something better than their predecessors; the cadmia and ladanum drugs are the best for cicatrization.
quote: Now most physicians abandon the drugs which from ancient times have given sufficient proof of themselves to all the best physicians and for this reason have become renowned

title: Andromachus arranged plasters by colour, writing 'another' sixteen times
summary: Galen faults Andromachus for listing sixteen green plasters headed only 'another', grouped by colour rather than power and without their uses.
quote: prefixing to each of them only this one word, "another", writing them all as differing from one another in power

title: Cold is hostile to nerves, so dry, near-neutral drugs are best
summary: Since putrefaction comes from moisture and heat, and Hippocrates rightly said cold is hostile to the nerves, Galen concluded that the best drug for nerve wounds dries and is neutral or somewhat hot.
quote: But reflecting again that cold has truly been said by Hippocrates to be hostile to the nerves

title: Older anatomists missed the triple Achilles tendon
summary: Galen says the tendon descending from the calf to the heel is made of three aponeuroses, a fact missed by anatomists older than him and now demonstrated by companions reading his anatomical books.
quote: the tendon descending from the calf appears both robust and thick, as being composed of three aponeuroses. This too had escaped the notice of the anatomists older than I

title: Dissect apes often; book learning makes 'helmsmen from a book'
summary: Galen insists anatomy must be learned by repeated dissection of apes; reading anatomical treatises is like the proverbial 'helmsmen from a book', and Empiricist chance-anatomy is nonsense.
quote: And still more nonsensical than this is learning through the anatomical treatises, which resembles those called, according to the proverb, 'helmsmen from a book'.

title: Anatomical Procedures: first to describe cutaneous nerve branches
summary: Galen says he described exactly, in his Anatomical Procedures, the small nerve branches that go only to the skin, which all earlier writers had omitted.
quote: matters about which I wrote accurately in the Anatomical Procedures, since they had been omitted by all before me.

title: Euphorbium loses strength over years; thapsia within two
summary: Thapsia is weak after a year and dead at two; good euphorbium keeps some power into the third or fourth year, weakens in the fifth and sixth, then dies. Age shows as a paler, yellower colour.
quote: For the latter becomes quite weak after a year, and expires completely once it has become two years old.

title: Galen's nerve-wound treatment 'by providence of the gods', unrecorded before
summary: Galen claims that none of the elders before him wrote down a whole course of treatment for nerve wounds, which he devised 'by a certain providence of the gods'.
quote: The whole course of treatment of those wounded in the nerves, which I devised by a certain providence of the gods, none of the elders before me wrote down.

title: Person's name 'Aphrodas' stands in an ingredient slot
summary: In Aphrodas's green plaster the list reads 'Aphrodas (?), 12 dr.' among the ingredients, which looks like a textual corruption, perhaps for an ingredient name.
quote: Aphrodas (?), 12 dr.; manna, 8 dr.; henna oil, an eighth of a kotyle. It is pounded together with it (?)
note: The Greek has Ἀφροδᾶς δραχ. ιβ΄, so the problem is in the transmitted text, not the draft. Unit failed the automatic check.

title: Fat quantity contradicts recipe (two pounds vs eight)
summary: The plain green plaster gives calf's fat 'two pounds', but Galen's comment speaks of 'the eight pounds of fat'; the commentary also mentions 'the pound of frankincense' though the recipe lists manna.
quote: I mean the eight pounds of fat, together with the eight of wax and the 12 of resin.
note: The Greek has the same inconsistency, so the error is in the Kühn text. Manna (λιβανωτοῦ μάννα) is frankincense powder, so that part may be all right.

title: Corrupt numeral in Galen's barbaros: '1 litra, 210 ounces'
summary: The oil quantity in Galen's own barbaros reads '1 litra, 210 ounces (σι΄)', which is impossible; the numeral is corrupt.
quote: oil, 1 litra, 210 ounces (σι΄).
note: The Greek reads οὐγγίας σι΄. Perhaps a corruption of a small fraction.

title: Asclepiades's 'Marcellas' assigned to internal remedies
summary: Here the text says the third book of Asclepiades's internal remedies is entitled Marcellas, contradicting K13.441-442 and K13.522-523, where Marcella is the series of external remedies and Mason the internal.
quote: in the third book of the internal [643] remedies (τῶν ἐντὸς φαρμάκων), which he also entitles Marcellas
note: Greek has ἐντὸς here; probably a corruption of ἐκτὸς. The nerve-wound plasters that follow are external remedies.

title: Untranslated 'τερμοτέρα' in the larch-resin description
summary: The draft leaves the Greek word τερμοτέρα untranslated among the qualities of the second kind of larch resin, and also lists 'hotter' separately.
quote: the other is more pungent than it and τερμοτέρα and more moist, and more unpleasant in smell and more bitter in taste and hotter.
note: Possibly a corruption of θερμοτέρα (hotter), which would duplicate 'hotter', or a form related to terebinth. Check the manuscripts.

title: 'Scraped verdigris 16 minae' implausible in Heras's polychrest
summary: In Heras's plaster for fractured limbs the draft gives scraped verdigris as 16 (ιστ΄) minae, against 1 mina of litharge and pitch, which is impossible; drachms are likely meant. The boiling instruction also has a doubled 'until (ἕως ἕως)'.
quote: of scraped verdigris 16 (ιστ΄) minae, of Cyprian copper one sixteenth of a mina
note: The Greek has ἰοῦ ξυστοῦ μνᾶς ιστ΄, so the error is in the transmitted numeral or unit, not the draft.

title: Implausible variant '45 minae' of wax in the 'Excellence' plaster
summary: In Andromachus's plaster 'the Excellence' the wax is '1 mina—others, 45 minae', which looks like a corrupt variant (perhaps 45 drachms).
quote: wax, 1 mina—others, 45 minae; sea-water, 3 cotylae.
note: The Greek has μνᾶς με΄ too, so the problem is in the transmitted text; probably drachms were meant.
